An elevated sedimentation rate is an important part of the diagnostic criteria for PMR. B
Low-dose prednisone (10-20 mg/day) is first-line therapy for treatment of PMR. B
The prognosis with treatment is excellent. B
Consider optimizing calcium and vitamin D from dietary sources or through supplementation and recommend lifestyle modifications for patients on chronic glucocorticoid treatment. C

background.definition: PMR is a vasculitic syndrome that manifests itself as severe stiffness and pain in the girdle muscles of the neck, shoulders, buttocks, and thighs. This condition is usually seen only in patients aged 50 years or greater.

list.listitem: 8.4/10,000 patients/year in the United Kingdom (95% CI, 8.3-8.6).
In one 9 year study in three general practices in the UK, the annual incidence was 11.3/10,000 patients aged 50 and over, with a median age of 75 years; 75% of patients were women.
5.9/10,000 patients/year in the United States (95% CI, 5.3-6.5), with 67% of cases occurring in women.
Incidence peaks between 70 and 80 years of age.
The overall prevalence in the United States is about 740 per 100,000 population: 532 for men and 925 for women.
Prevalence increases with age. summarizes the increasing prevalence for men, women, and all patients for different age groups.
The first year cost associated with care for PMR is between $2,233 and $27,712.
Patients with PMR are at increased risk of peripheral arterial disease (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.50 (95% CI, 1.53-4.08)) and myeloid malignancies (OR 1.73).
Left untreated, PMR can result in significant disability.
Unknown; may involve genetic predisposition (HLA-DR4), possibly triggered by infection (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, parvovirus B19, and Chlamydia pneumoniae are suspected).

A newer study has found immune complex-mediated neutrophil activation and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation to be central processes in the pathophysiology of PMR. Musculoskeletal symptoms appear to be associated with calprotectin elevation, while decrease in NETs appear to correlate with treatment response. These findings may help usher the development of more targeted therapies (eg, monoclonal antibodies) and soluble markers to monitor disease activity.
About 50% of people with giant cell arteritis (GCA) also have PMR. About 10% of people with PMR also have GCA.
Cellular immune response phenomenon involving T cells, macrophages, macrophage-derived inflammatory cytokines, antigen-presenting cells, and genetic human leukocyte antigen molecules.
Because of the duration of corticosteroid therapy, consider baseline bone density assessment, especially if bisphosphonates are not prescribed. C
To prevent glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, consider optimizing calcium and vitamin D from dietary sources or through supplementation and recommend lifestyle modifications. C

list.listitem: At least three different sets of diagnostic criteria are in use.

These are summarized in . Features common to these criteria include: proximal muscle pain and stiffness, elevated sedimentation rate, rapid improvement with low-dose corticosteroids, and absence of other conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory arthritis, malignant neoplasm, or muscle disease.

The typical patient with PMR is over 50 years of age and complains of acute, severe stiffness and pain in girdle muscles (neck, shoulders, buttocks, thighs). Shoulder pain is present in 70% to 90% of patients and hip and neck pain in 50% to 70% of patients. Physical findings are usually unremarkable.

Systemic symptoms of anorexia, depression, fever, malaise, night sweats, and weight loss are reported in about one-third of patients. One-half of patients have distal symptoms such as asymmetric arthritis, pitting edema and swelling of hands/wrists/ankles/feet, carpal tunnel syndrome.

The patient's symptoms, assessed systematically with the PMR Activity Scale (), should be used to monitor disease activity. In one study, associations with disease flare diagnosis were strongest for PMR-AS scores ≥9.35 (agreement with clinical diagnosis 92%, 95% 95% CI, 85.8%-95.7%).

It can be difficult to distinguish rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or other collagen vascular diseases from PMR early in the course. In a study of 116 patients with bilateral girdle pain for at least 1 month, a final diagnosis of RA was more likely in the presence of peripheral synovitis and proximal muscle atrophy, whereas weight loss was more common with PMR.
ESR is usually elevated. However, up to 20% of patients with PMR have normal sedimentation rates.
Mild anemia of chronic disease may be evident as well as mildly abnormal liver function tests in one-third of patients. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody testing are usually negative.
Subacromial and subdeltoid bursitis is commonly found in patients with PMR by using ultrasound or MRI.

In the UK incidence study above, the most common diagnostic features were proximal muscle pain (82%), elevated inflammatory markers (87%), clinical response to corticosteroids (91%) and normalization of inflammatory markers (81%).
The Polymyalgia Rheumatica Activity Scale, using five clinical variables, may be used to monitor disease activity (see ).
summarizes how to approach the patient with suspected PMR.
Low-dose prednisone (10-20 mg/day) is first-line therapy for treatment of PMR. B
Tapering prednisone can take years because of symptom flares. Tapering is based on patient symptom response. B
Monitoring and managing complications of corticosteroid therapy are essential. B

Because of the anticipated duration of therapy and risk of fractures, consider optimizing calcium and vitamin D from dietary sources or through supplementation and recommend lifestyle modifications. C

Low-dose prednisone (10-20 mg/day) usually improves PMR symptoms within days, with optimal results within several weeks. Tapering is individualized and can be reduced by 1 mg/day per week until most symptoms have resolved. Duration of therapy can last for years.

Methotrexate (10 mg weekly) and folic acid supplementation (7.5 mg/day) in addition to prednisone resulted in shorter duration prednisone treatment, reducing cumulative steroid exposure by 20% to 44%.
Adding infliximab to prednisone provides no additional benefit in patients with newly diagnosed PMR.

Sarilumab twice a month for 1 year hastens steroid tapering which reduces cumulative steroid dose and improves remission (which was low in both treatment and control groups). Neutropenia, diarrhea, and arthralgia were common adverse events. The annual drug cost is estimated to be $18,400. The cost per additional sustained response is more than $90,000, and it is unclear what the value is of the lower cumulative dose of prednisone.

Similarly, interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonist tocilizumab appears to hasten steroid tapering, reduce steroid use, and improve remission in patients with PMR on chronic steroids, based on a multicenter retrospective observation study.
Failure to respond to therapy requires reevaluation of diagnosis.
Based on a Cochrane review of 10 RCTs involving 811 patients, vitamin D does not appear to be beneficial for chronic pain, including PMR.
Treatment may last for up to several years.
The PMR Activity Score can be used to monitor disease activity. Scores less than 7 suggest low disease activity, scores of 7 to 17 suggest moderate activity, and scores >17 suggest high activity.

Reasons to consult a rheumatologist include failure to respond to initial steroid therapy; consideration of methotrexate use; provider inexperience with condition; atypical features; contraindications to corticosteroid therapy.

Long-term steroids are associated with several complications that warrant monitoring and treatment: osteoporosis, myopathy, hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol elevation, fluid retention, and emotional symptoms.
The prognosis is excellent with treatment. B

Relapses can be spontaneous and unpredictable. A cohort study with 384 patients found that higher initial corticosteroid dose and more rapid tapering were independent predictors of relapse. In another study, subclinical inflammation detected by US in the subacromial/subdeltoid bursae was persistent in most patients with PMR and was associated with a higher risk of relapses/recurrences. A third study found a 10-fold increase in risk of relapse for patients with PMR who had high interleukin-6 receptor levels combined with low hemoglobin values. B

Any evidence of temporal arteritis or giant cell arteritis (TA)?
PMR very likely; long-term, low-dose corticosteroids with gradual tapering over months to years.
High-dose steroids and temporal artery biopsy.
Consider other cause or coexisting conditions such as depression, osteoarthritis, or other degenerative conditions of the spine, shoulders, and hips.
